title: Looking back: the good potter
hookLine: a discourse we passed: the potter Ghatikara, who cared for his blind parents and kept the precepts

lines: THE BUDDHA SMILES BY THE ROAD.
A TOWN WAS HERE, LONG AGO.
cards: The Buddha is walking through Kosala with his monks when he stops at a certain spot by the road and smiles. Ananda knows a Buddha doesn't smile without a reason, so he asks.
Long ago, the Buddha says, there was a market town right here, and in it lived a potter named Ghatikara. That's the eighty-first discourse, passed by earlier on the way through the collection.
It's the story of a man with clay on his hands, and no robe, whom the text holds up as a model.

teach.h: THE FRIEND DRAGGED BY THE HAIR
teach.b: In the story, Ghatikara lives in the time of an earlier Buddha, Kassapa, and he's that Buddha's chief lay supporter.

His best friend is a young brahmin named Jotipala, who doesn't want to go see some shaven-headed recluse. Ghatikara drags him by the belt, and then, astonishingly, by the hair. A potter grabbing a brahmin by the hair!
Jotipala decides something serious must be going on, goes, listens, and becomes a monk. The text says that Jotipala was the Buddha himself, long before.
So the potter is the friend who got the future Buddha to his first teacher. But the heart of the story is how Ghatikara lives. He keeps the precepts.

He won't dig the ground himself, so he makes pots only from clay at broken riverbanks or heaps left by rats. He doesn't haggle: he sets his pots out and tells people to leave some rice or beans and take what they need.
And he looks after his parents, who are old and blind.
Once, while he's away, Kassapa Buddha comes for alms, finds no one home, and helps himself to rice from the pot. The blind parents are delighted when they hear.
Another time Kassapa's hut leaks in the rains, and his monks take the grass from Ghatikara's own roof to fix it.

His parents say: take it. The text says his roofless house stayed dry for three months. So a householder, not a monk, is the hero: care for elders, honest trade and steady virtue, done with your hands.
And that closes a week: Rahula under the tree, six sets of six, not inflamed, who to respect, review the road, see and stay.

how: Buddhist teaching across schools holds up care for parents as a great merit, and lay followers like Ghatikara are remembered as models of a householder's practice: refuge, precepts, honest livelihood and generosity.

s: he's a householder, a potter, who supports his blind parents.
in the story, Jotipala is the Buddha in an earlier life
the potter is the friend who brought the future Buddha to his teacher.
Ghatikara refused to dig the earth for clay himself
he used clay from broken riverbanks or heaps left by rats.

games.q: you're Ghatikara's old, blind parents. your son is away, and monks come asking for the grass from your roof to fix their teacher's leaking hut. what do you say?
o: wait until our son comes home.
games.why: they say take it, and the text says the roofless house stayed dry for the three months of rain.

practice: Bring to mind an older person in your life, a parent, a neighbor, someone frail, and picture their face. Breathe in their wellbeing, and let one small kindness for them come to mind: a call, a visit, a chore done for them.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Returning to a discourse we passed, and finding a quiet hero: a potter who cared for his parents and kept the precepts. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit upasaka: a lay follower, one who sits near. Ghatikara is the model upasaka.

carryVoice: Your line: the good potter. Clay on his hands, and a roofless house that stayed dry. Day five hundred eighteen.
